description:
Wesam Saad opens the obedience chapter with three clarifications. The subject is sanctification, rather than earning acceptance with God; believers are accepted in Christ. Christian obedience also comes from a changed heart, with new love, gratitude and a desire to please God. Finally, everyone still struggles with obedience. These truths frame the high standard that follows: failures should expose areas for growth, without becoming either a reason for despair or an excuse to stop pursuing holiness. The study therefore presents obedience as the direction of a life shaped by grace, rather than merely compliance with an external list of rules.

John 14:15 connects love for Jesus with keeping His commandments, and Matthew 22 extends that love to the whole person. Wesam distinguishes this from religious sentiment that produces strong feelings without obedience. He then reads Luke 9:22–23 together, placing self-denial and daily cross-bearing beside Jesus’s announced suffering and death. The marriage-vow illustration explains a settled commitment that must be lived out daily, even imperfectly. Following Christ means recognising Him as leader and Lord, rather than demanding that He follow personal preferences. The calling is personal and exclusive: family circumstances or changing emotions do not replace allegiance to the Saviour. The final question about persecution is left for further discussion.

questions.question: Is this lesson about earning salvation through obedience?
questions.answer: Wesam explicitly says it is about sanctification, not the means of becoming accepted by God. Acceptance is in Christ. The call to obedience therefore concerns how believers should grow, rather than a new set of conditions by which they earn entry into God’s kingdom.

questions.question: What makes Christian obedience more than following rules?
questions.answer: Wesam connects it with regeneration and a new heart. Love, gratitude and a desire to please God should motivate the outward action. The concern is therefore not merely whether someone performs an act, but whether the heart desires to honour the Lord.

questions.question: How does he connect love for Christ with obedience?
questions.answer: From John 14:15, Wesam says love for Jesus results in keeping His commandments. He then relates that to the command to love God with the whole person in Matthew 22. Strong religious feelings or an emotional response to music do not by themselves demonstrate that obedient love.

questions.question: How should a believer respond to falling short of that standard?
questions.answer: Wesam urges growth rather than despair. He acknowledges that believers struggle with unredeemed flesh, but says that weakness is not a justification for giving up. The new heart’s love for Christ should move a person towards fuller obedience, without treating each failure as proof that Christ has rejected them.

questions.question: Why does he read Luke 9:23 beside the preceding verse?
questions.answer: Luke 9:22 has Jesus announcing suffering, rejection, death and resurrection. Wesam therefore reads taking up the cross in that context, as readiness to follow Christ through suffering and shame, even at great cost. He treats it as a serious call to discipleship rather than a vague image for inconvenience.

questions.question: How can self-denial be a settled commitment and also a daily practice?
questions.answer: Wesam compares it with a marriage vow: a declaration establishes the intended direction, but that commitment must then be lived out over time. A believer’s failures do not make daily obedience unnecessary. The point is to continue on the path chosen in following Christ.

questions.question: Who is meant to lead in following Christ?
questions.answer: Wesam says Christ is the leader and Lord, while the believer follows Him. He challenges the idea that discipleship continues only while God answers as a person wishes or while obedience feels pleasant. Feelings do not provide forgiveness or reconciliation; Christ is the Saviour to whom allegiance belongs.

questions.question: Does a person’s calling to follow Christ depend on family members making the same choice?
questions.answer: Wesam emphasises the individual character of the call. Another family member’s inability or unwillingness to attend does not by itself cancel one’s own responsibility. He also explicitly recognises genuine care obligations, such as a bedridden spouse needing help. The point is personal allegiance to Christ, rather than automatic dependence on another person’s decision.
